task.goal: Develop a small museum display that makes a damaged everyday object meaningful without inventing its history.
hard_constraints: One display case, 150 words of label space and two weeks of staff time.
Unknown provenance must be marked as unknown; no fabricated owner story.
Compare visitor understanding and discomfort with a plain factual label.
task.available_resources: Object inspection notes and a curator interview.
task.expected_result: A responsible display concept and test.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Damage as a way to look
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the object's physical damage the reason to look closely. In the single case, position the object so one or two documented damaged features are visible without handling or treatment. A label of no more than 150 words directs attention to those features, explains their effect on ordinary use only where supported by inspection, and states: “Provenance and ownership history: unknown. The cause and date of this damage are unknown.” Separate observation from interpretation explicitly. End with a grounded invitation: “What does this damage let you notice about how the object was made or used?”

The mechanism is close observation: a familiar object becomes meaningful through its material construction and vulnerability, without needing a personal biography. Inspection notes supply the facts; the curator interview identifies what can responsibly be explained. This assumes the damage is visible and there is at least one accessible observation worth communicating. Damage alone cannot establish neglect, poverty, affection, or repair intentions. If the notes do not support an account of function, omit it.

One staff member drafts the label and prepares the case during week one; the curator checks every interpretive claim. Use week two for a visitor check and revision. No restoration, additional objects, or new historical research is required.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the interpretive label and a plain factual label in the same case across several short, balanced time blocks. Keep object position, typography, and label length similar. Invite a small convenience sample, aiming for 12 visitors per version. Ask what they noticed, what is known about the object's past, and whether any suggested history is certain; then ask for discomfort on a five-point scale and its reason. Code answers against the inspection notes. The concept fails its initial check if visitors notice no more supported detail, infer an owner story more often, or report greater discomfort without improved understanding. Treat results as formative, with visitor mix and small numbers limiting conclusions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: An object with an honest boundary
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Organize the case label around three explicit categories: “Observed,” “Possible,” and “Unknown.” Within the total 150-word allowance, give two or three observations drawn from the inspection notes, at most one useful interpretation supported by the curator interview, and a clear statement that provenance, ownership, and any undocumented cause of damage are unknown. If no interpretation is adequately supported, omit “Possible” rather than fill it with speculation. Display the object so visitors can check at least one observation themselves.

The mechanism is making the museum's evidential limits visible. The damaged everyday object becomes meaningful as an encounter with how knowledge is built and where it stops. Visitors can recognize that an institution's uncertainty is information, rather than a gap requiring an invented biography. This approach assumes the notes distinguish physical observations from deductions and that the curator can explain that distinction in ordinary language. It may feel procedural or emotionally distant; category headings alone will not guarantee understanding.

During week one, a staff member extracts claims from the notes and interview, assigns each a category, and asks the curator to challenge the assignments. Produce a simple printed label and install it beside the object in the existing case. Reserve week two for comparison and editing. The concept needs no visitor contributions, added collection material, or external research.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare this label with a plain factual label containing the same established object facts and the same explicit provenance disclosure. Alternate versions in balanced time blocks. Aim for 12 brief visitor interviews per version. Ask visitors to identify one observation, one uncertainty, and whether a suggested cause of damage is established; ask them to rate discomfort and explain it. Also ask whether the display helped them understand why the object deserves attention. Reject or revise the concept if headings increase confusion, speculation is recalled as fact, or evidential understanding improves only by making the object seem less worth viewing. These are exploratory responses, not proof of a general effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The visitor supplies the association
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a personal reflection prompt to connect the object to ordinary life while keeping its own biography explicitly unknown. The single case holds the object and a label of no more than 150 words. Begin with supported identification and visible condition, then state: “Its provenance and ownership history are unknown. We do not know how this damage happened.” Follow with: “Think of an everyday object whose damage changed how you saw it. Does that experience change what you notice here? Your association belongs to you; it is not evidence about this object's past.” Do not collect or exhibit visitor stories.

The mechanism is autobiographical association: visitors bring significance from their own experience rather than receive an invented owner narrative. It assumes that the object's everyday function is recognizable or can be explained from available evidence. It also assumes visitors can distinguish their associations from historical claims. The prompt may evoke loss, financial hardship, or distress, so participation stays optional and asks for no disclosure. Meaning may vary substantially, and some visitors will prefer factual interpretation.

In week one, use the inspection notes to establish the factual opening and the curator interview to check wording, accessibility, and unintended emotional pressure. Print the label and install it with the object; use week two for a small comparison and revision. No audio, response station, additional objects, or ongoing moderation is needed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the reflection label with a plain factual label in the same case, retaining the same factual opening and unknown-provenance statement. Aim for 12 visitors per condition across balanced time blocks. Ask what made the object meaningful, what they believe is known about its history, and whether the display prompted an unwanted personal memory. Collect a five-point discomfort rating without asking visitors to describe private experiences. The concept fails its initial check if visitors attribute their imagined stories to the object, report pressure to disclose, or show no greater sense of significance while discomfort rises. Report the range of reactions and uncertainty rather than treating average engagement as sufficient evidence of success.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Does damage disqualify an object?
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the object the focus of a curatorial judgment: can something damaged deserve museum attention? The mechanism is a change in the visitor’s role, from receiving an account to evaluating a collecting principle. Everyday usefulness and museum significance can differ; visitors consider that distinction without supplying a missing owner biography.

Use one case, with the object safely positioned and a single label under 150 words. Begin with identification and condition supported by the inspection notes. State: “Provenance and ownership history: unknown. Any undocumented date or cause of damage is also unknown.” Then ask: “Should damage count against an object’s place in a museum? Consider what this example can show and what its missing history prevents us from saying. You may decide that it deserves a place—or that the available evidence is insufficient.” Include one concise, curator-approved reason for displaying this particular object, explicitly presented as the museum’s present judgment.

This requires the curator interview to yield an honest selection rationale grounded in the object’s documented features. If no such rationale emerges, the concept is unsuitable. It does not establish rarity, representativeness, or historical importance. Its limit is that visitors may attend more to museum policy than to the object.

During week one, one staff member extracts the facts, interviews the curator, drafts the label, and obtains a claim-by-claim review. Use existing mounting and printed labels; reserve week two for visitor comparison and revision. No additional objects, research, or response installation is required.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate this label with a plain factual label across balanced short time blocks, keeping the same object position, established facts, and uncertainty disclosure. Aim for 12 brief interviews per version. Ask what the object demonstrates, what remains unknown, and why a museum might display it. Record whether explanations use supported features or invented history. Ask for discomfort on a five-point scale and an optional reason. Revise or abandon the concept if visitors merely repeat the question, invent biography more often, or feel judged for their answer without improved understanding. Treat this small convenience sample as formative evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Care happening now
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the museum’s present care of the object the display’s subject. A damaged everyday object becomes meaningful through a visible act of protection: visitors see how its condition changes what people must do for it now. This offers a documented present relationship without inventing a past owner.

Use the inspection notes and curator interview to identify one actual, condition-specific display decision—for example, supporting a weakened area or choosing an orientation that avoids pressure on a fracture. These are possibilities to verify, not facts to assume. Position the object safely in the single case so visitors can see the relevant feature and, where practical, its support. Do not deliberately expose it to risk for demonstration.

Within 150 words, identify the object using supported facts, explain the verified care decision in ordinary language, and state: “Provenance and ownership history: unknown.” Explicitly mark any undocumented cause or date of damage as unknown too. Connect the decision to its immediate purpose: what further damage the support is intended to prevent. Avoid claiming that the object was treasured, neglected, or repaired by an earlier owner.

The prerequisite is an existing or readily achievable care decision that the curator can substantiate within their expertise. If safe installation requires specialist assessment or a new custom mount beyond available resources, this concept is unsuitable. In week one, one staff member reviews the notes, interviews the curator, drafts the label, and prepares the approved installation using existing materials. Week two covers visitor checks and revision. The principal uncertainty is whether visitors find present care meaningful or merely technical.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Keep the safe installation identical while alternating the care label and a plain factual label across balanced short periods. Both labels include the same identification, condition facts, and unknown-provenance disclosure. Aim for ten brief visitor interviews per version. Ask what the damage changes about displaying the object, what remains unknown about its history, and what, if anything, makes it worth attending to. Record a five-point discomfort rating and an optional explanation, including whether the presentation feels overly sentimental. Revise or reject the concept if visitors cannot explain the care decision more accurately, infer earlier affection or ownership more often, or report increased discomfort without improved understanding. Treat this small sample as a formative check, not a reliable population estimate.

EXPAND.title: A familiar action interrupted
EXPAND.proposal:
Make the object meaningful through the ordinary action it once enabled, using an optional, contact-free gesture. The label identifies its supported function, invites visitors to imagine or gently mime one simple action, then asks how the documented damage might affect that action. Visitors can imagine the movement without moving. The object remains protected in the single case; no replica or handling station is required.

The mechanism is embodied understanding: connecting an everyday tool to a familiar movement can reveal why its condition matters. Unlike the prior close-observation route, this depends on mentally or physically performing an action rather than finding additional visible details. It requires reliable identification of the object's function and inspection evidence supporting a particular functional consequence. If either is missing, do not use this concept. Never imply that the gesture reconstructs an actual owner's behavior.

Use no more than 150 words for identification, condition, the invitation, and explicit disclosure: “Provenance and ownership history are unknown. The cause and date of the damage are unknown unless documented here.” Replace that final clause with the actual supported facts before printing.

In week one, a staff lead uses the notes and curator interview to select and verify one safe, accessible action, drafts the label, and installs the case. Avoid gestures requiring balance, strength, or imitation of injury. In week two, the lead runs the visitor check and revises or removes the prompt. The main uncertainty is whether the action adds understanding or merely creates a distracting activity.
EXPAND.experiment: The staff lead alternates three labels in balanced short blocks: plain factual, prior close-observation, and action prompt. All retain the same facts and provenance disclosure. Seek eight voluntary interviews per version. Ask visitors to explain the supported functional consequence and distinguish it from an unknown historical cause; record a five-point discomfort rating and whether participation felt physically or socially awkward. Stop the action prompt immediately if it encourages touching the case. Retain it only provisionally if functional understanding improves over the factual label and offers an advantage over close observation without greater discomfort or exclusion. Otherwise return to the simpler label. This small check can expose failure, not establish a general effect.

EXPAND.title: Why give this object a case?
EXPAND.proposal:
Make the museum's present choice to display the object the source of significance. Interview the curator about why this particular damaged everyday object merits attention now. Write a label of at most 150 words that identifies the object, states its documented condition and unknown provenance, and gives one concrete, attributed reason for selecting it. End with an optional question: “Does that reason justify giving this object space in a museum?”

The mechanism is institutional accountability: visitors encounter a real, current decision about what deserves preservation and attention. Meaning comes from evaluating that decision, so a recovered owner biography is unnecessary. Unlike the prior evidence-category route, the central question concerns the museum's values and allocation of attention, rather than how confidently it knows historical facts.

This requires the curator to articulate an honest reason specific enough to debate. A newly formed interpretation is acceptable if identified as the curator's current view; it must not be presented as the original acquisition rationale. Do not imply rarity, representativeness, or historical importance unless the supplied materials support those claims. If no defensible selection reason emerges, abandon this route.

One staff lead extracts the factual core from the inspection notes and drafts the attributed rationale during week one. The curator verifies both its accuracy and its status as a present judgment. Install only the object and label in the single case. Week two covers interviews and revision. No visitor voting apparatus or additional research is needed. The principal risk is that institutional justification overwhelms the object or makes visitors feel that disagreement is unwelcome.
EXPAND.experiment: The staff lead compares the proposal with a plain factual label and the prior Observed/Possible/Unknown label, alternating balanced viewing blocks and seeking eight interviews per version. Ask visitors why the object is displayed, which statements concern its history versus the curator's present judgment, and whether they consider it worth attention. Record discomfort on a five-point scale, including whether the question felt like a test with a correct answer. Stop or revise if visitors repeatedly convert the curator's rationale into an unsupported historical fact. Keep the concept only if it improves understanding of significance over the factual label and adds value beyond the evidence-category version sufficient to justify the interview and attribution work. Report disagreement as a legitimate response, not a failed visitor.

EXPAND.title: A real choice about care
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a genuine unresolved care decision to give the damaged object present consequences. Ask the curator whether the available inspection notes support two feasible approaches—for example, retaining the present appearance or undertaking a particular intervention—with a meaningful tradeoff. The single-case label, within 150 words, describes that actual choice, explains one supported benefit and cost of each approach, and invites visitors to consider which they would favor. State explicitly that provenance and ownership are unknown and that any undocumented damage cause remains unknown.

The mechanism is responsibility: the object matters because choices made now can preserve or alter something that cannot simply be replaced. This differs from the prior personal-association route because visitors consider consequences for this object rather than supply memories from their own lives. It also differs from explaining the museum's selection decision: the visitor weighs alternative future actions with material consequences.

This route is conditional. The curator must confirm that both options are genuinely feasible using existing knowledge. Do not invent a restoration dilemma, imply that damage necessarily needs repair, or suggest that visitor preferences authorize treatment. If the evidence supports only one safe course, use another concept. No treatment takes place during the trial.

In week one, the staff lead and curator verify the decision and its consequences, prepare the label, and install the object safely in its existing case. In week two, the lead gathers responses and checks misunderstandings. The label states that care remains the museum's responsibility. The principal uncertainty is whether the dilemma creates meaningful concern or avoidable anxiety about the object's safety.
EXPAND.experiment: The staff lead alternates this label, a plain factual label, and the prior personal-reflection label in balanced blocks, seeking eight voluntary interviews per version. Ask visitors to explain one real tradeoff, identify what remains unknown, and say whether they believe the object is currently endangered or their answer determines treatment. Measure perceived significance and discomfort separately. Stop the dilemma version if it repeatedly creates a false impression of imminent damage or binding visitor authority. Retain it only provisionally if visitors understand the tradeoff and find the object more meaningful than with the factual label, with an advantage over personal reflection that warrants the extra complexity. If significance gains accompany confusion or increased distress, return to the factual label. Findings remain formative.

EXPAND.title: Damage as a way to look—with a visibility gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Damage as a way to look.” Preserve its mechanism: the object's documented damage directs attention to construction, ordinary function, and material vulnerability. Add one operational gate before installation: the staff lead checks the proposed feature from normal visitor positions through the closed case. A useful inspection observation may be too small, obscured, or dependent on specialist knowledge to support this display.

Use the inspection notes and curator interview to select one supported feature. Within existing safe mounting options, position it visibly and draft a label of at most 150 words identifying the object, directing attention to that feature, and explaining only documented consequences. Explicitly state that provenance and ownership are unknown and identify any unknown cause or date of damage. Do not infer emotional or social history.

The lead owns preparation until the curator accepts the factual claims and positioning. If the feature cannot be seen without unsafe repositioning, try one other documented feature; if neither works, install the plain factual label. The factual version is also the fallback if preparation is interrupted or review cannot finish in week one. No treatment or new equipment is required.

Compared with the source, this prevents an otherwise sound interpretation from depending on inaccessible evidence. It adds a short viewing check but may narrow the available interpretation. Whether it increases significance remains uncertain.
EXPAND.experiment:
During week two, the staff lead alternates the interpretation and plain factual label in balanced short blocks, keeping object position and typography constant and both labels within 150 words. Seek about ten voluntary interviews per version. Ask visitors to point out the relevant feature without touching, explain its supported significance, and name what remains unknown. Ask whether the object seems worth attention, then collect discomfort on a five-point scale and its reason.

After the first four interpretation interviews, stop and use the factual label if two visitors cannot locate the feature or mistake an undocumented damage story for fact. Otherwise finish the small comparison. Retain provisionally only if supported understanding and significance improve without increased historical misconception; examine discomfort separately. Small convenience samples can identify failures but cannot establish general superiority.

EXPAND.title: Personal association with an explicit way to decline
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “The visitor supplies the association.” Preserve autobiographical association as the mechanism: a visitor's own experience can give an unfamiliar everyday object significance without supplying its biography. The consequential gap is that an optional prompt alone gives a visitor little direction after an unwanted memory begins.

Change the working label to provide two immediately usable paths. After the supported identification, condition, and explicit unknown-provenance statement, write: “If you wish, think of an everyday object whose damage changed its meaning for you. You need not share the memory. You can also simply consider this object's everyday purpose. Your associations are not evidence about its history.” Fit the entire label within 150 words. Do not solicit, record, or display personal stories.

In week one, the staff lead drafts from the notes and curator interview; the curator checks factual accuracy and whether the alternative path makes sense for this object. This requires reliable identification of its everyday purpose. If that prerequisite fails, or review is interrupted, use the plain factual label. Keep that replacement ready throughout week two.

Compared with the source, the added sentence offers a concrete way to continue viewing after declining reflection, at a small cost in label space. Compared with factual interpretation, the route may produce more personal significance but still carries greater emotional risk. It cannot promise that difficult memories will be avoided.
EXPAND.experiment:
In week two, the staff lead alternates this label with a plain factual label containing the same identification, condition, and uncertainty disclosures. Seek about ten brief voluntary interviews per condition. Ask what made the object meaningful, what is known about its history, and whether visitors felt free to skip the personal prompt. Collect a five-point discomfort rating and ask whether the display prompted an unwanted memory, without requesting its content.

If a visitor reports feeling pressured to recall or disclose something personal, replace the reflection label for the remainder of that block and review the wording before reuse. If that response recurs after one revision, retire the prompt. Also revert if visitors repeatedly treat associations as historical evidence. Judge significance and understanding alongside discomfort, rather than letting higher engagement cancel distress. Report these as formative findings.

EXPAND.title: An everyday object encountered as sculpture
EXPAND.proposal:
Use aesthetic reclassification as a new mechanism: invite visitors to encounter the object as a composition before considering its everyday identity. Meaning comes from a present visual experience, without requiring a recovered biography, personal memory, or explanation of what caused the damage.

In the single case, use an existing safe orientation that presents a clear silhouette. A label of at most 150 words begins: “For a moment, look at this as a sculpture: its shape, balance, surface, and gaps.” Then give the supported everyday identification and condition. State explicitly that provenance and ownership are unknown, along with any undocumented damage cause or date. Explain that the invitation is a way of looking today; it does not establish artistic intention or historical art status.

The staff lead uses the notes and curator interview in week one to verify identification and select a safe presentation. No treatment, special lighting, additional objects, or commissioned imagery is needed. The curator must confirm that the damage does not make a purely aesthetic invitation inappropriate given the available evidence. If identification is uncertain, say so; if no visually accessible presentation or responsible framing emerges, use the factual label.

This removes the assumption that significance must begin with historical or functional explanation. Compared with a factual label, it may make an ordinary object worth sustained attention, but risks aestheticizing damage or implying artistic intention. Those benefits and risks are untested.
EXPAND.experiment:
During week two, the staff lead alternates the aesthetic invitation and a plain factual label in balanced blocks, holding the case arrangement constant. Seek about ten voluntary interviews per version. Ask what makes the object worth viewing, what visitors understand about its everyday identity and damage, and whether they believe it was made as art. Collect a five-point discomfort rating and ask whether the presentation seems to trivialize damage.

Pause the aesthetic version if two of its first four interviewees infer artistic intention or an invented history. Permit one wording revision within the two-week limit; if the misunderstanding recurs, revert to the factual label. Retain only provisionally if visitors find supported significance while retaining factual understanding, without a recurring discomfort concern. This small check tests whether aesthetic reframing adds value sufficient to justify its interpretive risk.
